# Unit 2: Organization, personnel, premises, equipment and raw materials

GMP rests on four foundations: trained people, suitable buildings, fit equipment and good starting materials. If any one is weak, testing at the end cannot rescue the product. This unit follows the order of the syllabus: organization and personnel, premises (including sterile areas), and equipment and raw materials. The Indian requirements come from Schedule M of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, which closely follows WHO GMP. Schedule M was revised in December 2023; always check the current text on cdsco.gov.in for exact figures.

## 2.1 Organization

A manufacturing unit must have an organisation chart that shows who reports to whom, with written job descriptions for every key post.

```text
Typical organisation of a pharmaceutical plant

                     Managing Director / Plant Head
                                  |
      +-----------+---------------+---------------+------------+
      |           |               |               |            |
  Production   Quality         Quality        Engineering   Stores /
   Head        Assurance Head  Control Head   (maintenance)  Warehouse
      |           |               |
  Supervisors  QA officers     Analysts,
  Operators    (IPQA, document  microbiologists
               control, audits)

QA and QC heads are independent of the Production head.
```

**Key points**

- The heads of **Production** and **Quality** (QA/QC) must be different people, and neither reports to the other. This separation stops pressure to release a batch that should be rejected.
- The **Authorised Person / person responsible for batch release** (under the revised Schedule M this role sits within the quality unit) certifies that each batch was made and tested as required before it is released for sale.
- Key posts must be held by full-time staff with the qualifications and experience that the licence rules require (for example a degree in pharmacy or chemistry for the technical staff named on the licence).
- Duties must not overlap in a way that leaves gaps, and deputies must be named for absences.

**Responsibilities of the main heads**

| Head of Production | Head of Quality Control | Head of Quality Assurance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ensure products are made and stored as per approved documents (MFR, SOPs) | Approve or reject starting materials, packaging materials, intermediates and finished products | Approve SOPs, master documents and changes |
| Approve production instructions and make sure they are followed | Approve specifications, sampling instructions and test methods | Run the quality system: deviations, CAPA, change control, self-inspection |
| Check that batch records are completed and signed before they go to QA | Make sure all tests are done and records checked | Release or reject batches after review of the batch record |
| Make sure premises and equipment are maintained, and validations done | Ensure validation of methods and calibration of instruments | Oversee validation, training, vendor approval, complaints and recalls |
| Make sure staff are trained | Manage retention samples and stability studies | Conduct product quality review and audits |

Shared responsibilities: authorising written procedures, monitoring the factory environment, plant hygiene, process validation, training, vendor approval, and storage conditions.

## 2.2 Personnel

### 2.2.1 Qualifications and responsibilities

- Enough staff with the right education, training and experience for each task.
- Each person's duties written in a job description; nobody given so many duties that quality suffers.
- Key personnel (production head, QC head, QA head) have the qualifications laid down in the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules.

### 2.2.2 Training

| Type of training | Who | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Induction | All new joiners | GMP basics, company policy, hygiene, safety |
| Job-specific (on-the-job) | Operators, analysts | SOPs of their equipment and tasks, under supervision |
| GMP refresher | All staff, at set intervals | Updates in GMP, case studies, past deviations |
| Special | Staff in sterile areas, people handling potent, toxic or sensitising materials | Aseptic technique, gowning, containment |
| Visitors and contractors | Untrained people entering production | Briefing and supervision |

Training needs are identified, a yearly plan is made, sessions are given, and **effectiveness is assessed** (written test, observation). Records of every training are kept in the person's training file.

### 2.2.3 Hygiene

1. **Medical examination** before employment and at regular intervals; eye test for people doing visual inspection.
2. Anyone with an infectious disease, open lesion or skin wound on an exposed surface must not handle products; staff must report illness.
3. **Protective clothing** suited to the area: overalls, head cover, beard cover, face mask, gloves, shoes; sterile gowns for aseptic areas.
4. **No eating, drinking, chewing, smoking**, storing food or personal medicines in production, storage and laboratory areas.
5. No jewellery, wrist watches, cosmetics or loose items in production areas.
6. Hand washing and sanitising; direct contact of hands with exposed product avoided.
7. Change rooms with step-over benches, and gowning procedures displayed.
8. Visitors and untrained people kept out, or supervised and gowned.

### 2.2.4 Personal records

Each employee has a personal file: application and appointment letter, qualifications, experience, job description, medical fitness records, training records and assessments, and authorisation for specific tasks (for example, sign-off authority). These records show an inspector that the person is competent for the work they sign for.

## 2.3 Premises

### 2.3.1 Location and surroundings

- Away from open sewers, drains, public lavatories, dusty roads and factories that give off smoke, dust or odour.
- Protected against entry of insects, birds, rodents and other animals.
- Surroundings kept clean, with good drainage.

### 2.3.2 Design and construction

| Feature | Requirement and reason |
| --- | --- |
| Walls and ceilings | Smooth, impervious, free from cracks, easy to clean and disinfect; coving at wall–floor and wall–ceiling joints so dust cannot settle |
| Floors | Smooth, hard, impervious, non-slip, chemical-resistant (for example epoxy) |
| Doors and windows | Flush, well fitted; windows in clean areas sealed; no uncleanable ledges |
| Pipes, ducts, lights | Designed so they do not create recesses; services reached from outside the clean area where possible |
| Drains | Of adequate size with trapped gullies; avoided in aseptic areas |
| Lighting | Adequate for the work |
| Space | Enough to place equipment and materials in an orderly way, with no mix-ups |

### 2.3.3 Plant layout

Rooms are placed in the logical order of operations so that materials move in one direction, people and materials have separate routes, and clean and less clean areas do not cross.

```text
One-way flow (simplified layout for oral solid dosage forms)

Receiving -> Quarantine -> Sampling -> Approved stores -> Dispensing (weighing)
     -> Granulation -> Drying -> Blending -> Compression -> Coating
     -> Primary packing -> Secondary packing -> Finished goods (quarantine)
     -> Release -> Dispatch

Separate: QC laboratory, change rooms, toilets (not opening into production),
          rest rooms, maintenance workshop, rejected-material store (locked)
```

**Layout principles:** separate areas for receiving, quarantine, approved, rejected and returned materials; a separate sampling booth; segregated or dedicated facilities for highly sensitising products (for example penicillins, cephalosporins), certain hormones, cytotoxics and biologicals; air locks between areas of different cleanliness; QC laboratories separate from production; ancillary areas (canteen, toilets) not opening directly into production.

### 2.3.4 Maintenance and sanitation

- Written sanitation programme: what to clean, how, how often, with which agent, and who is responsible.
- Validated cleaning and disinfection; disinfectants rotated in clean areas to avoid resistant organisms.
- Pest control programme (rodent baits outside, insect-o-cutors at entrances), with records.
- Preventive maintenance of the building: repair of cracks, peeling paint and leaks; maintenance must not put products at risk.
- Waste removed regularly to a designated area in closed containers.

### 2.3.5 Environmental control and utilities

**Heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC)** controls temperature, relative humidity, particle count, air movement and pressure differences. It is one of the most important GMP systems.

| Control | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Filtration (pre-filters, fine filters, HEPA terminal filters in clean areas) | Remove particles and microbes |
| Pressure differential | Air flows from cleaner to less clean area; containment rooms may be kept at lower pressure to keep powder in |
| Air changes per hour | Dilute and remove particles |
| Temperature and RH | Product stability (hygroscopic, effervescent products need low RH) and operator comfort |
| Dust extraction at source | Control of cross-contamination during dispensing and compression |

**Utilities** that touch the product must be qualified and monitored:

- **Water systems:** potable water → purified water (for oral preparations, cleaning) → water for injections (for parenterals, made by distillation or another method the pharmacopoeia allows), stored and circulated to avoid microbial growth, tested regularly.
- **Compressed air and nitrogen:** oil-free, filtered, tested for particles, moisture and microbes where they contact the product.
- **Steam:** clean steam for sterilisers.
- Electric supply with backup for critical equipment.

### 2.3.6 Sterile areas

Sterile products are made in clean rooms graded by the number of airborne particles. Revised Schedule M uses Grades A to D, as in WHO and EU GMP.

| Grade | Typical use | Max particles ≥0.5 µm per m³ (at rest) | Approximate ISO class at rest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | High-risk operations: filling, open ampoules and vials, aseptic connections (usually under unidirectional airflow) | 3,520 | ISO 5 |
| B | Background environment for Grade A in aseptic preparation and filling | 3,520 | ISO 5 |
| C | Less critical steps, for example preparing solutions to be filtered | 352,000 | ISO 7 |
| D | Handling components after washing, less critical steps | 3,520,000 | ISO 8 |

Limits for particles ≥5.0 µm, the "in operation" limits and microbial action limits differ between versions of the guidance; take them from the current Schedule M or the WHO/EU annex on sterile products.

**Requirements for sterile areas**

- Entry only through air locks and change rooms, with stepwise gowning (sterile garments in Grade B).
- Unidirectional (laminar) airflow over Grade A operations, with a set air velocity.
- Positive pressure towards less clean areas (a difference of the order of 10–15 Pa between adjacent rooms of different grades is commonly used).
- No sinks or drains in Grade A/B areas; minimal equipment; smooth sealed surfaces.
- Interlocked doors in air locks, pass boxes for materials, HEPA filters tested for integrity.
- **Environmental monitoring:** non-viable particle counts, viable counts by settle plates, active air sampling, contact plates and glove prints; temperature, RH and pressure differentials recorded.
- Aseptic process simulation (media fill) to show the process can produce sterile product.
- Minimum number of people inside; their movements slow and controlled.

### 2.3.7 Control of contamination

| Type | Sources | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cross-contamination (one product into another) | Dust, residues on equipment, air recirculation, people, shared tools | Campaign manufacture with cleaning, dedicated facilities for sensitising drugs, air locks and pressure cascades, dust extraction, validated cleaning, closed systems |
| Microbial contamination | People, water, air, raw materials, equipment | Hygiene, gowning, HEPA filtration, water system control, sanitisation, microbial limits on raw materials |
| Particulate / foreign matter | Fibres, glass, metal, paint flakes | Smooth surfaces, sieves and metal detectors, inspection |
| Mix-ups | Similar labels, many products in one area | Line clearance, status labels, segregation, one product per line |

## 2.4 Equipment

### 2.4.1 Selection

Equipment must be suited to its purpose and installed so that it:

- Has the capacity and precision the process needs (for example a balance of the right range and readability).
- Has product-contact parts that do not react with, add to or absorb from the product (usually stainless steel 316L for contact parts; gaskets of approved materials).
- Can be cleaned easily, with no dead legs or crevices; can be dismantled for cleaning; clean-in-place where possible.
- Does not shed lubricants or particles into the product.
- Meets safety and environmental needs.

### 2.4.2 Purchase specification (user requirement specification)

The **user requirement specification (URS)** is written before purchase. It states: purpose and capacity, operating ranges, materials of construction, cleanability, safety features, controls and data-recording needs (data integrity for computerised equipment), utilities needed, documents to be supplied (manuals, drawings, material certificates, calibration certificates), training and after-sales support, and qualification support (IQ/OQ protocols). The URS is the basis for design qualification (Unit 5).

### 2.4.3 Maintenance

- Written **preventive maintenance** programme with a schedule for each item; records in the equipment log book.
- Calibration of measuring instruments at set intervals against traceable standards, with calibration labels showing the next due date.
- **Equipment log books** record use (product, batch), cleaning, maintenance and breakdowns.
- **Status labels**: "Cleaned", "To be cleaned", "Under maintenance", "Out of order". Defective equipment removed or clearly labelled.
- Repairs done so they do not affect the product; equipment re-qualified after major repair or modification.

## 2.5 Raw materials and stores

### 2.5.1 Purchase specifications for raw materials

Every starting material (active ingredient, excipient, packaging material) has an approved specification stating:

- Name, internal code, pharmacopoeial or in-house reference.
- Description, identification, assay, impurities and other tests with limits.
- Grade and particle size (where it matters).
- Approved suppliers (manufacturers) only.
- Storage conditions, retest period or shelf life, and precautions.
- Packing requirements and labelling expected from the supplier.

**Vendor (supplier) approval:** materials are bought only from approved suppliers. Approval rests on samples tested against specification, a questionnaire, a site audit for critical materials, and later on performance (rejection rate, timeliness). Each delivery should come with the supplier's certificate of analysis, but the company still tests it (at least identity for every container of the active, according to its sampling plan).

### 2.5.2 Maintenance of stores

```text
Material path in the stores

Receipt (check documents, containers, seals, labels; clean containers)
   -> Goods receipt note, own label with internal code/receipt number
   -> QUARANTINE (yellow label)
   -> Sampling in a sampling booth under laminar airflow
   -> QC testing
   -> APPROVED (green label)  or  REJECTED (red label, locked area)
   -> Issue by FEFO/FIFO against a requisition
```

**Good stores practice**

- Enough space, separate areas for quarantine, approved, rejected, recalled and returned goods.
- Storage conditions controlled and recorded (room temperature, cool, cold room 2–8 °C as required); temperature-mapped areas.
- Materials on pallets or racks, off the floor and away from walls, for cleaning and pest control.
- Flammable materials and solvents in a separate fire-safe store; narcotics and psychotropics in locked storage as the law requires.
- Printed packaging materials (labels, cartons) stored securely and issued against counts to prevent mix-ups.
- Stock records (bin cards or computer system) that reconcile receipts, issues and balance.
- Expired materials or materials past their retest date are not issued without re-testing.

## Remember

- Production head and quality heads are different people, independent of each other.
- Personnel: qualified, trained (induction, job-specific, refresher, assessed), medically fit, hygienic, with personal records.
- Premises: suitable site, smooth cleanable finishes, one-way flow, segregation for penicillins and other sensitisers, HVAC with pressure cascades, qualified utilities.
- Sterile areas: Grades A–D; at rest ≥0.5 µm limits 3,520 / 3,520 / 352,000 / 3,520,000 per m³; Grade A under unidirectional airflow with Grade B background; environmental monitoring and media fills.
- Equipment: fit for purpose, cleanable, non-reactive (SS 316L), URS before purchase, preventive maintenance, calibration, log books and status labels.
- Raw materials: approved specification and approved vendors; quarantine → sampling → approved/rejected labels; FEFO/FIFO.

# Unit 3: Quality control of packaging materials and Good Laboratory Practices

The container is part of the medicine. A good tablet in a leaky strip, or an injection in glass that sheds alkali, will fail before its expiry date. The first half of this unit covers the quality control tests for containers, rubber closures and secondary packing materials. The second half covers Good Laboratory Practice (GLP). The headings of the GLP topic follow the US FDA regulation 21 CFR Part 58 (Good Laboratory Practice for Nonclinical Laboratory Studies), and the same ideas appear in the OECD Principles of GLP and in Schedule L-1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (Good Laboratory Practices for testing laboratories). Test limits change between editions, so take exact figures from the current Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) when you need them.

## 3.1 Packaging: terms and requirements

| Term | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary packaging | In direct contact with the product | Glass vial, ampoule, bottle, blister foil, rubber stopper |
| Secondary packaging | Holds the primary pack; gives protection, information and branding | Carton, leaflet, label, shipper's inner box |
| Tertiary packaging | For bulk handling and transport | Corrugated shipper, pallet, stretch wrap |

A good container protects the product from light, moisture, oxygen, microbes and physical damage; does not react with, add to (leach) or take up (sorb) anything from the product; is compatible with sterilisation if needed; and is easy to use, tamper-evident and economical.

## 3.2 Quality control tests for glass containers

**Types of glass (IP)**

| Type | Composition | Hydrolytic resistance | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type I | Borosilicate glass (neutral glass) | Highest | Most parenteral preparations, including those that must be autoclaved, blood products |
| Type II | Soda-lime glass with a surface treatment (de-alkalised surface) | High surface resistance | Many aqueous parenterals with pH below 7, if stable |
| Type III | Ordinary soda-lime glass | Moderate | Non-aqueous parenterals, powders for injection, oral and topical preparations |
| Type IV (general purpose soda-lime) | Soda-lime glass | Low | Oral and topical products only |

**Tests**

| Test | Purpose and principle |
| --- | --- |
| Hydrolytic resistance – powdered glass test | Glass is crushed and sieved to a set particle size, heated with purified water in an autoclave, and the alkali released is titrated with dilute acid. Measures the resistance of the glass itself (used to identify Type I and Type III) |
| Hydrolytic resistance – surface glass test (water attack test) | Containers are filled with water and autoclaved; the alkali released from the inner surface is titrated. Tests the surface, so it distinguishes Type II (treated surface) from others |
| Arsenic test | Limit test on the water extract of glass for injection containers, because arsenic can be present in glass batch materials |
| Light transmission test | For coloured (amber) glass: the percentage of light transmitted between about 290 and 450 nm must be below the limit, to show light protection |
| Thermal shock test | Containers are moved between hot and cold water baths to check they do not crack during sterilisation or cooling |
| Internal bursting pressure test | For containers that must stand internal pressure (aerosols, carbonated liquids) |
| Annealing test | Examination under polarised light (polariscope) to detect strain left in the glass |
| Dimensional checks and visual inspection | Neck finish, capacity, wall thickness; defects such as cracks, stones, bubbles, cords |

## 3.3 Quality control tests for plastic containers

Plastics (polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC, PET, polystyrene) are light and unbreakable but can be permeable to gases and water vapour, can leach additives and can sorb drugs or preservatives.

| Test | What it checks |
| --- | --- |
| Description and identification (for example infrared spectrum) | That the right polymer is used |
| Leakage test | Containers filled, closed and inverted or squeezed; no leakage |
| Collapsibility test (for containers that must be squeezed to empty, for example eye drops, IV bags) | Container empties the required proportion of its contents under pressure |
| Clarity / transparency of the container | Contents can be inspected visually (for parenteral containers) |
| Water vapour permeability | Gain or loss of weight of filled containers stored under set conditions; tells moisture protection |
| Clarity and colour of aqueous extract | Containers are extracted with water; extract must be clear and colourless |
| Physicochemical tests on the extract | Non-volatile residue, residue on ignition, heavy metals, buffering capacity, absorbance (UV), pH change |
| Biological (toxicity) tests | Systemic injection test and intracutaneous (irritation) test in animals using extracts; for parenteral and ophthalmic containers |
| Sorption / compatibility study | Loss of drug or preservative into the plastic during storage with the actual product |

Blister and strip packs are checked for foil thickness, heat-seal strength, pinholes, and leak test by vacuum (blue dye or methylene blue test: packs are immersed in dye under vacuum, then examined for dye entry).

## 3.4 Quality control tests for rubber closures

Rubber (elastomeric) closures seal vials and are pierced by needles. They contain the polymer plus fillers, vulcanising agents, accelerators, antioxidants and pigments, all of which can leach.

| Test | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Identification (for example IR of the extract, ash, density) | Correct elastomer formulation |
| Sterilisation | Closures must survive the stated sterilisation without change |
| Penetrability | The force needed to push a standard needle through the closure must not exceed the limit |
| Fragmentation (coring) | After repeated piercing with a needle, the number of rubber fragments seen in the vial must not exceed the limit |
| Self-sealability (resealing) | After piercing, the closure reseals so that the vial does not leak (tested by immersing in a dye solution under pressure) |
| Physicochemical tests on extract | Appearance of extract, acidity or alkalinity, absorbance, reducing substances, volatile sulfides, ammonium, heavy metals, residue on evaporation |
| Biological tests | Toxicity tests on extracts for parenteral use |
| Dimensions and hardness | Fit with the vial neck and seal |

Compatibility of the closure with the product (sorption of preservatives such as chlorocresol, leaching of extractables) is shown in stability studies.

## 3.5 Quality control of secondary packing materials

Secondary materials are mostly paper, board and corrugated fibreboard.

| Test | Material | Principle and purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grammage (GSM) | Paper, board | Mass per square metre; consistency of the material |
| Thickness (caliper) | Paper, board | Measured with a micrometer |
| Bursting strength | Board, corrugated box | Pressure needed to rupture the material (Mullen tester); resistance to rough handling |
| Compression strength | Corrugated boxes | Load a box can carry before collapse; decides safe stacking height |
| Cobb test | Paper, board | Water absorbed by a set area in a set time; resistance to moisture |
| Moisture content | Board | Too much makes boxes weak; too little makes them brittle |
| Tearing and folding endurance | Cartons, leaflets | Withstands use without tearing at folds |
| Drop test and vibration test | Packed shipper | Product survives dropping and transport vibration |
| Print and text checks | Labels, cartons, leaflets | Matches the approved artwork: name, strength, batch, dates, legal text, barcode; colour shade against standard |

Printed materials have the highest risk of **mix-ups**, so they are checked against the approved "master" artwork, stored securely, counted on issue and reconciled after packing, and excess printed batch-coded material is destroyed with records.

## 3.6 Good Laboratory Practice (GLP): introduction

**Definition.** GLP is a quality system covering the organisational process and the conditions under which **non-clinical** health and environmental safety studies are planned, performed, monitored, recorded, archived and reported.

**Why GLP began:** in the 1970s, inspections in the USA found non-clinical (animal) safety studies submitted to the FDA that had poor or even fabricated data. This led the FDA to issue GLP regulations (21 CFR Part 58, in force from 1979). The OECD Principles of GLP followed, so that data from one member country are accepted in others.

**Aim:** to make study data **reliable, reproducible, traceable and auditable**, so a regulator can reconstruct exactly what was done.

**Scope:** toxicity studies (acute, sub-acute, chronic), carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, mutagenicity, safety pharmacology, toxicokinetics and similar studies done to support marketing or clinical-trial applications. GLP does not cover basic exploratory research or clinical studies on humans (those follow GCP).

**India:** Schedule L-1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules lays down GLP requirements for drug testing laboratories. India is also a full member of the OECD Mutual Acceptance of Data system for GLP through its national GLP compliance monitoring programme (check the current status with the National GLP Compliance Monitoring Authority).

## 3.7 The parts of the GLP regulation (21 CFR Part 58)

### 3.7.1 General provisions (Subpart A)

States the **scope** (non-clinical laboratory studies that support applications for research or marketing permits), gives **definitions**, and says that the testing facility must allow **inspection** by the regulator and that a sponsor must state whether each study was done under GLP.

**Key definitions**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Nonclinical laboratory study | In vivo or in vitro experiment in which test articles are studied prospectively in test systems under laboratory conditions to find their safety |
| Test article | The drug, additive or product being tested |
| Control article | Anything other than the test article given to the test system for comparison (placebo, vehicle, reference) |
| Test system | Any animal, plant, microorganism or part of them (cells, tissues) to which the article is given |
| Sponsor | The person or company that starts and supports the study |
| Testing facility | The place where the study is done |
| Study director | The individual with overall responsibility for the technical conduct of the study |
| Quality assurance unit (QAU) | Any person or group designated to monitor the study for compliance; independent of the study staff |
| Raw data | Original records and observations that are needed to reconstruct the study |
| Specimen | Material taken from the test system for examination |

### 3.7.2 Organization and personnel (Subpart B)

**Personnel:** education, training and experience suited to their tasks; a current summary of training and experience plus a job description for each person; enough staff; hygiene and protective clothing; anyone ill excluded from contact with test systems.

**Testing facility management:** designates the study director (and replaces them if needed), ensures a QAU exists, ensures test and control articles are tested for identity and strength, ensures personnel, resources, facilities and methods are available, and ensures deviations reported by the QAU are acted on.

**Study director:** the single point of control. Ensures the protocol is followed and approved changes documented; all data are recorded accurately; unforeseen events are noted with corrective action; test systems are as described in the protocol; GLP is followed; and raw data, documents, specimens and the final report go to the archives at the end.

**Quality assurance unit:**

- Keeps a **master schedule sheet** of all studies at the facility (test article, test system, nature of study, start date, current status, sponsor, study director).
- Keeps copies of all protocols.
- **Inspects** each study at intervals suited to it, and reports problems to the study director and management.
- Reports periodically on each study's status.
- Checks that no deviations were made from protocols or SOPs without proper authorisation.
- **Reviews the final report** to make sure it describes the methods accurately and reflects the raw data, and signs a QA statement in the report.
- Its people are not involved in conducting the study they monitor.

### 3.7.3 Facilities (Subpart C)

- Size, construction and location suited to the work; separation so that activities do not interfere with each other.
- **Animal care facilities:** separate rooms for different species, for different studies, for quarantine of new animals, and for isolating diseased animals; rooms for handling biohazardous materials; storage of feed, bedding and supplies away from pests; safe waste disposal.
- Separate areas for receipt and storage of test and control articles, and for mixing them with carriers (for example feed).
- **Laboratory operation areas** separate for each kind of work.
- **Specimen and data storage facilities (archives)** with limited access.
- Administrative and personnel areas.

### 3.7.4 Equipment (Subpart D)

- Equipment of appropriate design and capacity, located for operation, inspection, cleaning and maintenance.
- Regular inspection, cleaning, maintenance, testing, calibration and standardisation, as per written SOPs that name the person responsible and the remedy when equipment fails.
- Written records of all these operations and of any non-routine repair.

### 3.7.5 Testing facilities operation (Subpart E)

- **Standard operating procedures** for all routine methods: animal room preparation, animal care, receipt and identification of test and control articles, test system observations, laboratory tests, handling of moribund or dead animals, necropsy, specimen collection and identification, histopathology, data handling and storage, equipment maintenance and calibration, animal transfer and identification.
- SOPs available in each work area; deviations authorised by the study director and documented; historical files of SOPs kept.
- **Reagents and solutions** labelled with identity, concentration, storage requirements and expiry date.
- **Animal care:** proper housing, feeding, handling and identification (each animal identified uniquely, for example by ear tag); newly received animals isolated and checked; analysis of feed and water for contaminants that could interfere with the study.

### 3.7.6 Test and control articles (Subpart F)

- **Characterisation:** identity, strength, purity and composition of each batch known and documented, with methods of synthesis or source; stability determined.
- Each container labelled with name, code or batch number, expiry date where appropriate, and storage conditions.
- **Handling:** procedures for receipt, storage, distribution and accountability so that contamination, deterioration and mix-ups are avoided; records of quantities received and used.
- **Mixtures with carriers** (for example drug in feed): uniformity, concentration and stability of the mixture determined by analysis at intervals.

### 3.7.7 Protocol for and conduct of a nonclinical laboratory study (Subpart G)

Every study has an approved written **protocol** that states:

1. Descriptive title and purpose of the study.
2. Identification of the test and control articles.
3. Name of the sponsor and name and address of the testing facility.
4. Number, body weight range, sex, source, species, strain and age of the test system.
5. Procedure for identifying the test system.
6. Experimental design and methods to control bias.
7. Type and frequency of tests, analyses and measurements.
8. Records to be kept.
9. Dose levels (in mg/kg or other units), method and frequency of administration, and route.
10. Statistical methods.
11. Date of approval by the sponsor and dated signature of the study director.

**Conduct:** the study follows the protocol; specimens are identified by test system, study, nature and date of collection; all data are recorded directly, promptly and legibly in ink, dated and signed or initialled by the person entering them; any change to an entry must not obscure the original, must state the reason, and must be dated and signed. Computer-entered data must identify the person responsible and keep an audit trail.

### 3.7.8 Records and reports (Subpart J)

**Final report** contains: name and address of the facility, study dates, objectives and procedures as in the protocol with any changes, statistical methods, test and control article identification and characterisation, stability information, methods used, test system details, dosage and route, unforeseen circumstances, a description of how data were transformed, a summary and analysis of the data with conclusions, names of the study director and scientists, reports of each scientist involved, the location of stored specimens and raw data, and the **QA statement**. It is signed and dated by the study director. Corrections after signing are made as signed and dated amendments.

**Storage and retrieval of records:** all raw data, documentation, protocols, specimens and final reports are kept in **archives** for orderly storage and rapid retrieval, under an individual responsible for the archives, with limited access. The regulation sets minimum retention periods tied to the dates of approval or submission of the application; quote them from the current regulation if asked.

### 3.7.9 Disqualification of testing facilities (Subpart K)

The purpose of disqualification is to exclude from consideration data from studies done by a facility that has failed to comply with GLP, when that failure affects the validity of the data.

**Grounds:** the facility failed to comply with one or more GLP requirements; the non-compliance adversely affected the validity of the studies; and other lesser measures (warnings, rejection of individual studies) have not been or will not be adequate.

**Consequences:** the regulator notifies the facility and gives an opportunity for a hearing; studies done at a disqualified facility are presumed unacceptable unless shown otherwise; the regulator may inform other agencies and sponsors; it may also take legal action. **Reinstatement** is possible when the facility shows in writing, and on inspection, that it has corrected the problems and will comply.

```text
GLP at a glance

People (management, study director, QAU, trained staff)
  + Places (separate facilities, animal rooms, archives)
  + Things (calibrated equipment, characterised test articles, labelled reagents)
  + Paper (SOPs, approved protocol, raw data, final report, QA statement)
  = Reliable, reconstructable non-clinical safety data
```

## Remember

- Glass: Type I borosilicate (best), Type II surface-treated soda-lime, Type III soda-lime, Type IV general purpose. Powdered glass test checks the bulk glass; surface (water attack) test checks the inner surface.
- Plastics: leakage, collapsibility, water vapour permeability, extract tests, biological tests, sorption.
- Rubber closures: penetrability, fragmentation (coring), self-sealability, extract tests, biological tests.
- Secondary packing: GSM, bursting strength, compression strength, Cobb test, moisture, drop and vibration tests, artwork check.
- GLP = 21 CFR Part 58 / OECD principles / Schedule L-1; for non-clinical safety studies.
- Study director = single point of control; QAU = independent monitor with master schedule, inspections and final-report review.
- Protocol must be approved before the study starts; raw data recorded promptly, in ink, signed and dated; changes must not obscure the original.
- Disqualification only when non-compliance affects data validity and lesser measures are not enough; reinstatement is possible.

# Unit 4: Complaints, recalls and documentation

When a medicine leaves the factory, quality assurance does not end. Patients, pharmacists and doctors report problems; some goods come back; sometimes a batch must be pulled out of the market. All of this depends on good records, because a batch that cannot be traced cannot be recalled. This unit covers complaints, returned goods, recalls and waste disposal, then the main documents of a pharmaceutical plant: the master formula record, the batch record, SOPs, audits, quality review and distribution records.

## 4.1 Complaints

A **complaint** is any written, electronic or oral report that a product may be defective, unsafe or not performing as expected.

**Sources:** patients, doctors, pharmacists, hospitals, distributors, sales staff, regulators.

**Types of complaints**

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Quality (product) complaints | Broken or chipped tablets, discolouration, foreign particles, leaking bottles, wrong count, cracked ampoules |
| Packaging and labelling complaints | Wrong label, missing batch number or expiry, misprint, leaflet missing |
| Medical / adverse event complaints | Lack of effect, unexpected side effects (passed to the pharmacovigilance team) |
| Counterfeit suspicion | Pack looks different from genuine product |
| Commercial complaints | Short supply, damaged transit cartons, wrong quantity |

### 4.1.1 Handling and evaluation of complaints

A written SOP names a responsible person (usually in QA) and lays out these steps:

```text
Receive complaint -> log it (number, date, complainant, product, batch, nature)
   -> acknowledge the complainant
   -> classify by seriousness (critical / major / minor)
   -> obtain the complaint sample if possible
   -> investigate:
        review batch manufacturing and packing records
        test retention (reserve) samples of the same batch
        test the complaint sample
        check other complaints on the same batch or product (trend)
        check deviations, changes and stability data
   -> find the root cause
   -> decide action: corrective and preventive action (CAPA),
      and whether a recall or regulator notification is needed
   -> reply to the complainant
   -> close the complaint; review complaints regularly for trends
```

**Classification by seriousness**

| Class | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Critical | Could cause serious harm or death | Wrong drug in pack, sterile product contaminated |
| Major | Could reduce effect or cause harm, but less serious | Low assay, dissolution failure |
| Minor | Little risk to the patient | Small print fault on the carton, minor surface spots |

**Evaluation points:** Is the defect real? Is it due to manufacture, storage, transport or misuse? Does it affect only one pack, the whole batch or other batches? Is there a risk to patients?

**Records:** each complaint is recorded with all findings, the decision and the action taken; complaint records are reviewed regularly (and in the product quality review) to spot repeated problems. If the investigation suggests a counterfeit, or a serious defect, the licensing authority is informed.

## 4.2 Handling of returned goods

**Returned goods** are products sent back from the market by distributors or customers: expired stock, damaged goods, near-expiry stock, wrongly supplied stock, or products under complaint or recall.

**Procedure**

1. Receive in a separate, locked "returned goods" area; record product, batch, quantity, reason, source and date.
2. Keep under quarantine until QA decides.
3. QA evaluates: nature of product, storage conditions it may have met in the market (for example temperature for heat-sensitive products), time out of the company's control, condition of the packs, remaining shelf life, and the reason for return.
4. Decision:
   - **Return to saleable stock** only if there is no doubt about quality: original packs unopened and in good condition, storage known to be proper, enough shelf life, QC check satisfactory (rarely done for products that need cold storage).
   - **Reprocessing / repacking** only under an approved procedure, if quality is not affected.
   - **Destruction** in all other cases.
5. Record the decision and action; returns are trended as a sign of problems.

## 4.3 Product recall

A **recall** is the action to remove from the market a batch or batches of a product that are defective, or suspected to be, or that violate the law. A recall may be started by the company (voluntary) or ordered by the regulator.

**Reasons for recall:** contamination (microbial, particulate, cross-contamination), wrong labelling or mix-up, sub-standard assay or dissolution, stability failure before expiry, sterility failure, a serious adverse reaction linked to the batch, a product declared spurious or adulterated, or a licence problem.

**Classes of recall** (based on health hazard; the class terms are those used by CDSCO's recall guidance, which follows international practice)

| Class | Hazard | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Class I | Reasonable probability that use will cause serious adverse health effects or death | Wrong active ingredient, contaminated injection, sterility failure |
| Class II | May cause temporary or reversible health effects, or a remote chance of serious harm | Sub-potent life-saving drug, dissolution failure |
| Class III | Not likely to cause adverse health effects | Minor labelling defect, wrong pack colour |

The guidance also sets the time within which each class of recall must reach each level and the depth of recall (wholesaler, retailer, consumer). Check the current CDSCO recall guidelines for these timelines.

**Recall procedure**

```text
Decision to recall (recall committee: QA head, production head, regulatory,
                    sales/distribution, medical)
   -> classify the recall and decide depth (wholesale / retail / patient level)
   -> inform the licensing authority
   -> use distribution records to find every consignee of the batch
   -> send recall letters / messages (product, batch, reason, what to do)
   -> public notice for Class I recalls where needed
   -> recalled stock received, kept separately in a locked area
   -> reconcile: quantity made vs distributed vs returned vs remaining in market
   -> check effectiveness of the recall
   -> investigate root cause and take CAPA
   -> destroy recalled goods under supervision; record
   -> final report to the authority
```

The recall system must be able to work quickly at any time, including outside working hours, and its effectiveness should be tested periodically by **mock recalls**.

## 4.4 Waste disposal

| Waste | Disposal |
| --- | --- |
| Rejected, returned and recalled products, expired stock | Destroyed under QA supervision by a method that prevents reuse or diversion (crushing, incineration or through an authorised waste handler), with a destruction record witnessed by responsible people |
| Printed packaging material with batch details or obsolete artwork | Shredded or burnt, recorded |
| Hazardous chemical waste, solvents | Through authorised hazardous-waste treatment facilities, as per the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules and pollution control board consent |
| Biomedical waste (for example from microbiology labs) | Segregated, decontaminated (autoclaved) and disposed of under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules |
| Effluents | Treated in an effluent treatment plant to meet pollution control board norms |
| Narcotic and psychotropic products | Destroyed as the special law requires, with the authority informed |

Waste must be kept in closed, labelled containers in a designated area away from production, and removed regularly.

## 4.5 Documentation: purpose and general rules

"If it is not written down, it did not happen." Documents define the system (specifications, master formulae, SOPs) and records prove that it was followed (batch records, logs).

**Purpose of documentation**

- Gives clear written instructions so work is done the same way each time.
- Lets every batch be traced: what was used, who did what, when, with which equipment.
- Provides evidence for audits, inspections and investigations.
- Supports training and continual improvement.

**Good documentation practice (GDP), also summed up as ALCOA principles:** data must be **A**ttributable (who did it), **L**egible, **C**ontemporaneous (recorded at the time), **O**riginal and **A**ccurate. ALCOA+ adds complete, consistent, enduring and available.

**Rules**

1. Documents are designed, prepared, reviewed and distributed with care; approved, signed and dated by authorised people.
2. Written in clear, unambiguous language; title, number, version and effective date on each.
3. Entries made in indelible ink at the time of the activity; no blank spaces left (strike through unused space).
4. Corrections: single line through the wrong entry so it stays readable, correct value written beside, signed, dated and the reason given. No overwriting, erasing or correction fluid.
5. Controlled copies issued and obsolete versions withdrawn.
6. Electronic records protected by access control, backup and audit trails.
7. Records kept for the period required by law.

## 4.6 Master Formula Record (MFR)

The **Master Formula Record** is the master document, prepared and approved for each product and batch size, that lays down how the product is to be made. Each batch record is copied from it.

**Contents of an MFR**

| Section | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Product details | Name, dosage form, strength, generic name, product code, description, batch size |
| Signatures | Prepared by, checked by, approved by (production and QA), with dates |
| Formula | Name and quantity of every ingredient per unit and per batch, including overages with reasons; ingredients that disappear in processing (for example water) also listed |
| Specifications | References to specifications of raw and packing materials |
| Equipment | List of equipment and their capacities |
| Manufacturing instructions | Step-by-step method with process parameters (times, temperatures, speeds), precautions, in-process controls and their limits |
| Expected yield | Theoretical yield and acceptable limits at stages |
| Packing instructions | Pack size, packing materials with codes, quantities, line clearance, printing details, specimen of printed materials |
| Storage | Storage conditions and precautions |

## 4.7 Batch Formula Record / Batch Manufacturing Record (BMR)

The **batch record** (called the batch formula record in the syllabus; usually the Batch Manufacturing Record, BMR, plus a Batch Packing Record, BPR) is a copy of the current MFR issued for one batch and filled in while the batch is made. It is the history of that batch.

**Contents**

- Product name, batch number, batch size, dates of start and completion, manufacturing and expiry dates.
- Line clearance records before each stage (no material or document of the previous product remains).
- Each raw material: name, quantity required, quantity actually weighed, its receipt/QC number, signatures of the person weighing and the checker.
- Equipment used and its cleaning status.
- Each processing step with actual parameters, times, signatures of operator and supervisor.
- In-process control results.
- Yields at each stage and reconciliation; explanation of any deviation.
- Packing: packing materials issued, used, returned and destroyed (reconciliation of printed materials), specimen of the printed batch coding.
- QC test results, and final review and release by QA.

| MFR | BMR |
| --- | --- |
| Master document, one per product and batch size | Record of one particular batch |
| Instructions: what should be done | Evidence: what was actually done |
| Prepared once, revised through change control | Issued for each batch |
| Blank spaces for data do not apply | Filled in at the time of each step |

Under the older Schedule M, batch records were kept for at least one year after the expiry date of the batch. Confirm the retention period in the revised Schedule M.

## 4.8 Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)

An **SOP** is an authorised written procedure giving instructions for performing routine operations, not necessarily specific to one product (for example operation and cleaning of a tablet press, calibration of a balance, handling of complaints, gowning).

**Format of an SOP**

```text
+--------------------------------------------------------+
| Company name / logo         | SOP title                |
| SOP no.: QA/001  Version: 02 | Effective date / Review date |
| Department                  | Page x of y              |
+--------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. Objective (purpose)                                   |
| 2. Scope                                                 |
| 3. Responsibility                                        |
| 4. Accountability                                        |
| 5. Procedure (numbered steps)                            |
| 6. Precautions / safety                                  |
| 7. Abbreviations and definitions                         |
| 8. References                                            |
| 9. Annexures / formats                                   |
| 10. Revision history                                     |
| Prepared by | Checked by | Approved by (QA) - sign/date  |
+--------------------------------------------------------+
```

**SOP lifecycle:** drafting by the user department → review → approval by QA → training of users → issue of controlled copies → periodic review (for example every two or three years) → revision through change control, with the old version withdrawn and archived.

## 4.9 Quality audit

A **quality audit** is a systematic, independent and documented examination of whether quality activities and results comply with planned arrangements, and whether these arrangements are carried out effectively and are suitable to achieve objectives.

| Type | Who audits whom | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Internal audit (self-inspection) | Company's own trained team audits its departments | Check GMP compliance and find gaps before an inspector does |
| External / supplier (vendor) audit | Company audits its suppliers and contract manufacturers or labs | Approve and monitor vendors |
| Third-party / regulatory inspection | Regulator (CDSCO, state licensing authority, WHO, foreign agencies) or certification body audits the company | Licensing, certification, export approval |

**Audit process:** plan (schedule, scope, checklist) → opening meeting → collect evidence (observing, interviewing, checking records) → classify observations (critical, major, minor) → closing meeting → written report → auditee's CAPA plan → follow-up to verify closure.

## 4.10 Quality review and quality documentation

**Product quality review (PQR)** (also called annual product review) is a regular, usually yearly, review of each product to confirm the process is consistent and the specifications are still right. It covers:

- Review of starting and packing materials, especially from new sources.
- Critical in-process controls and finished product results (with trends).
- All batches that failed specification and their investigations.
- Significant deviations, non-conformances and CAPA.
- Changes made to processes or methods.
- Stability programme results.
- Complaints, returns and recalls.
- Adequacy of previous corrective actions.
- Qualification status of equipment and utilities.

The PQR leads to decisions on whether revalidation, changes or other action are needed.

**Management review** is a periodic review by senior management of the whole quality system (audit results, complaints, PQR outcomes, CAPA status) under ICH Q10 and ISO 9001.

**Hierarchy of quality documentation**

```text
            /\
           /  \       Level 1: Quality manual / quality policy
          /----\
         /      \     Level 2: Quality procedures (site master file,
        /--------\             validation master plan, SOPs)
       /          \   Level 3: Work instructions, specifications,
      /------------\           MFR, test methods
     /              \ Level 4: Records and forms (BMR, logs,
    /----------------\         analytical reports, certificates)
```

**Site master file:** a document prepared by the manufacturer containing specific information about its quality management, production and control activities at that site (general information, personnel, premises and equipment, documentation, production, QC, distribution, complaints, recalls, self-inspection).

## 4.11 Reports and documents

| Document | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Specifications | For raw materials, packing materials, intermediates, finished products: tests and limits |
| Certificate of analysis (CoA) | QC test results for a batch, with a conclusion of pass or fail, signed by an authorised person |
| Analytical records / test reports | Raw data of each test: weights, readings, chromatograms, calculations |
| Equipment log books | Use, cleaning, maintenance, calibration |
| Deviation reports | Unplanned departure from an approved procedure, its investigation and impact |
| Change control records | Proposed change, evaluation, approval, implementation, effectiveness check |
| CAPA records | Root cause, corrective action, preventive action, effectiveness check |
| Out-of-specification (OOS) reports | Investigation of results that fail specification |
| Validation protocols and reports | Plan and results of qualification and validation |
| Training records | Who was trained on what, when, with assessment |

## 4.12 Distribution records

**Distribution records** show for each batch to whom it was sent, how much and when. They must be kept so that any batch can be recalled quickly and completely.

**Contents:** product name, batch number, quantity dispatched, date of dispatch, name and address of consignee, invoice or delivery number, mode of transport, and for cold-chain products the transport conditions.

**Good distribution points:** dispatch on FEFO (first expiry, first out) basis; vehicles clean and suitable; temperature-sensitive goods in validated cold-chain containers with temperature records; records kept at least as long as batch records.

## Remember

- Complaints: log → classify (critical/major/minor) → investigate (records, retention samples, trends) → root cause → CAPA → reply → close; trend regularly.
- Returned goods: quarantine; resale only if there is no doubt about quality; otherwise reprocess under procedure or destroy.
- Recall: Class I (serious harm or death), Class II (temporary or reversible harm), Class III (no harm likely); uses distribution records; reconcile; mock recalls; inform the authority.
- MFR = master instructions; BMR = record of one batch; SOP = routine operations; ALCOA for records.
- Audits: internal (self-inspection), supplier, regulatory/third party.
- Product quality review = yearly review of all data on a product; site master file describes the site.
- Distribution records make recall possible; dispatch by FEFO.

# Unit 5: Calibration, validation and warehousing

Testing a sample tells you about that sample. Validation tells you that the process, equipment and method will give the right result every time, so that a tested sample can stand for the whole batch. Calibration makes sure the instruments that measure the process tell the truth. This unit covers the definitions and principles of calibration, qualification and validation, the types of validation, the validation master plan, two worked examples (pH meter calibration and UV-visible spectrophotometer qualification), analytical method validation, and finally good warehousing practice and materials management.

## 5.1 Definitions

| Term | Definition (in plain words) |
| --- | --- |
| Calibration | The set of operations that establish, under stated conditions, the relationship between the values shown by an instrument and the known values of a reference standard, and adjust it if needed |
| Qualification | Action of proving and documenting that equipment or ancillary systems are properly installed, work correctly and actually lead to the expected results. It is part of validation, applied to equipment, utilities and facilities |
| Validation | Action of proving and documenting, in line with GMP, that any procedure, process, equipment, material, activity or system actually leads to the expected results consistently |
| Verification | Confirmation by examination and evidence that specified requirements have been met (for example verifying a pharmacopoeial method in your own lab) |

Simple way to remember: **we calibrate instruments, qualify equipment and validate processes and methods.**

## 5.2 Calibration: general principles

1. Every instrument used for measurement in production and QC is listed in a calibration master list with its identification number, range, accuracy needed and frequency of calibration.
2. Calibration follows a written SOP, against **reference standards traceable** to national or international standards (in India, through the National Physical Laboratory or an accredited calibration laboratory).
3. The standard used is more accurate than the instrument being calibrated.
4. Calibration covers the range in which the instrument is used.
5. Results are recorded; acceptance limits are set in advance.
6. A label on the instrument shows the date of calibration, the next due date and who did it.
7. If an instrument is found **out of calibration**, it is labelled "out of calibration", not used, repaired and recalibrated; the impact on results obtained since the last good calibration is investigated.
8. Calibration may be done in-house or by an outside agency (preferably NABL-accredited for that parameter).

**Typical instruments calibrated:** balances, pH meters, thermometers and temperature sensors, pressure gauges, timers, UV-visible spectrophotometers, HPLC, dissolution apparatus, disintegration testers, hardness testers, autoclaves and ovens (temperature probes).

## 5.3 Qualification

```text
V-model of qualification

 User requirement specification (URS) ----------------> Performance qualification (PQ)
      \                                                       /
   Design qualification (DQ) ---------------------> Operational qualification (OQ)
          \                                             /
     Functional / design specifications --> Installation qualification (IQ)
                         \                       /
                          ---- Build / supply ----

Left side: what we need and how it is designed.
Right side: proof that what was delivered meets each level.
```

| Stage | Question it answers | Typical checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Design qualification (DQ) | Is the proposed design suitable for its intended purpose? | Design and specifications compared with the URS and GMP needs; materials of construction; cleanability |
| Installation qualification (IQ) | Has it been delivered and installed correctly? | Equipment received as ordered, components, drawings, manuals, utilities connected, materials of construction certificates, calibration of built-in instruments, SOPs drafted |
| Operational qualification (OQ) | Does it work as intended across its operating ranges? | Function of controls, alarms, interlocks, speeds, temperatures at upper and lower limits, "worst case" conditions, without product |
| Performance qualification (PQ) | Does it perform consistently in actual use with product or simulated product? | Runs with product or placebo, repeated (commonly three consecutive runs), meeting acceptance criteria |

After major repair, relocation or modification, **requalification** is done. Periodic review confirms equipment remains in a qualified state.

## 5.4 Validation

### 5.4.1 Importance of validation

- Builds quality into the product instead of relying on end testing alone.
- Assures that every batch is consistent, because a sample cannot detect all defects (for example sterility tests examine only a few units).
- Reduces rejects, reprocessing and complaints, saving cost.
- Reduces risk to patients.
- Is a legal requirement of GMP (Schedule M, WHO, US FDA, EU).
- Supports process improvement and makes changes safer through revalidation.

### 5.4.2 Scope of validation

| Area | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Process validation | Granulation, compression, coating, mixing, filling, sterilisation (autoclave, dry heat), aseptic filling (media fill), lyophilisation |
| Cleaning validation | Proof that cleaning removes residues of product and detergent and controls microbes, to an acceptable limit |
| Analytical method validation | Assay, impurity, dissolution and identification methods |
| Equipment and facility qualification | Production and laboratory equipment, clean rooms, HVAC |
| Utility qualification | Purified water, water for injections, compressed air, nitrogen, clean steam |
| Computer system validation | Software controlling processes or holding GMP records (data integrity) |
| Transport and storage validation | Cold chain, warehouse temperature mapping |
| Packaging validation | Sealing of blisters, container closure integrity |

### 5.4.3 Types of process validation

| Type | When done | Description | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prospective validation | Before a new product or process is released for sale | Planned studies on (commonly) three consecutive batches under a pre-approved protocol; batches released only after the report is approved | The preferred approach |
| Concurrent validation | In exceptional cases (for example low-volume products, urgent supply) | Validation done during routine production; batches may be released one by one after testing, while data are collected | Must be justified and approved by QA |
| Retrospective validation | For products long in production, not validated before | Review of historical batch records, in-process and final test data of many batches (often 10–30) to show consistency | No longer accepted as the normal approach for new work by most regulators |
| Revalidation | After changes or periodically | Repeat of validation after a change in formula, process, equipment, site, batch size or supplier, or after trends show drift | Driven by change control |

**Modern lifecycle approach** (as described in US FDA process validation guidance, 2011): Stage 1 process design, Stage 2 process qualification (including PQ of the process), Stage 3 continued process verification during routine production.

**Typical process validation protocol contents:** objective, scope, responsibilities, description of process and equipment, critical process parameters and quality attributes, sampling plan (where, how many, when), tests and acceptance criteria, number of batches, deviation handling, and report format.

### 5.4.4 Validation master plan (VMP)

A **VMP** is a high-level document that summarises the company's overall philosophy, intentions and approach to validation, and lists what will be validated, by whom and when.

**Contents of a VMP**

1. Introduction and validation policy of the site.
2. Scope: products, processes, facilities and systems covered.
3. Organisation: validation team and responsibilities.
4. Plant, process and product description (brief).
5. Specific process considerations: critical parameters.
6. List of items to be qualified or validated (facilities, utilities, equipment, processes, cleaning, methods, computer systems).
7. Key acceptance criteria.
8. Documentation format: protocols and reports, numbering.
9. Required SOPs.
10. Planning and scheduling (time plan, priorities).
11. Change control and revalidation policy.
12. Training needs.

## 5.5 Calibration of a pH meter

**Principle.** A pH meter measures the potential difference between a glass electrode (sensitive to H+ ions) and a reference electrode. The response is linear with pH; the theoretical slope is about 59.16 mV per pH unit at 25 °C. Calibration with standard buffers sets the zero point (intercept) and the slope.

**Standard buffers (commonly used, values at 25 °C)**

| Buffer | Approximate pH |
| --- | --- |
| Potassium hydrogen phthalate (0.05 M) | 4.01 |
| Mixed phosphate (equimolar KH2PO4 and Na2HPO4) | 6.86 |
| Sodium borate (borax, 0.01 M) | 9.18 |

Many laboratories also use commercial certified buffers of pH 4.00, 7.00 and 10.00. Use the pharmacopoeial values for the buffer and temperature in use.

**Procedure**

1. Switch on and allow to warm up as per the SOP; check the electrode is filled and clean.
2. Rinse the electrode with purified water and blot dry (do not rub).
3. Set the temperature or use automatic temperature compensation; buffers at about 25 °C.
4. Immerse in the neutral buffer (pH about 7) and standardise (set the zero/offset).
5. Rinse, immerse in the acidic buffer (pH about 4) and set the slope.
6. Rinse, immerse in the alkaline buffer (pH about 9.2) and check the reading (or set as third point).
7. Read each buffer again as a sample; the reading must agree with the stated value within the limit set in the SOP (commonly ±0.05 pH unit).
8. Record the slope; acceptance commonly 95–105% of theoretical (follow the SOP).
9. Record results and affix the calibration label. Daily calibration before use is usual; a full calibration with more checks is done at longer intervals.

**Precautions:** fresh buffers within expiry; do not pour used buffer back; keep the glass bulb wet (store in the recommended solution); calibrate with buffers that bracket the expected sample pH.

## 5.6 Qualification of a UV-visible spectrophotometer

The pharmacopoeia lists performance checks that show the instrument gives correct wavelength and absorbance readings. Exact limits must be taken from the current IP.

| Parameter | Usual method | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control of wavelength (wavelength accuracy) | Holmium oxide filter or holmium perchlorate solution (sharp peaks at known wavelengths, for example near 241, 287, 361 and 536 nm), or emission lines of a deuterium or mercury lamp | The wavelength scale is correct; tolerance is tighter in the UV range than in the visible range |
| Control of absorbance (photometric accuracy) | Potassium dichromate dried and dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid (about 0.005 M), read at 235, 257, 313 and 350 nm; specific absorbance compared with the stated values | Absorbance readings are accurate |
| Limit of stray light | Potassium chloride solution (about 1.2% w/v), absorbance read near 198–200 nm must be greater than a stated value (2.0) | Little light of other wavelengths reaches the detector, so high absorbances are reliable |
| Resolution (spectral bandwidth) | Toluene (0.02% v/v) in hexane: the ratio of absorbance at the maximum near 269 nm to the minimum near 266 nm must be not less than the stated value | The instrument can separate close peaks |
| Cells | Matched cuvettes checked with the same solvent | Cell errors are small |

**IQ** of the instrument covers delivery, installation, software and documents; **OQ** covers the tests above plus noise, baseline flatness and drift; **PQ** checks performance in routine use (for example a known standard measured regularly).

## 5.7 General principles of analytical method validation (ICH Q2(R2))

**Purpose:** to show that an analytical procedure is suitable for its intended use. The current guideline is ICH Q2(R2), adopted with the related guideline ICH Q14 on analytical procedure development; check ich.org for the version in force.

**Validation characteristics**

| Characteristic | Meaning | Usual approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specificity / selectivity | Ability to measure the analyte without interference from impurities, degradants, excipients | Analyse placebo, spiked samples, stressed (degraded) samples; peak purity |
| Accuracy | Closeness of the result to the true value | Recovery of known amounts, commonly 3 levels × 3 replicates across the range |
| Precision | Closeness of results of repeated measurements | **Repeatability** (same analyst, short time: at least 9 determinations over the range or 6 at 100%), **intermediate precision** (different days, analysts, equipment), **reproducibility** (between laboratories); expressed as % RSD |
| Linearity (response) | Results proportional to concentration in the range | At least 5 concentrations; correlation coefficient, slope, intercept |
| Range | Interval between upper and lower concentration with suitable accuracy, precision and linearity | Assay typically 80–120% of the test concentration |
| Detection limit (DL/LOD) | Lowest amount that can be detected, not necessarily quantified | Signal-to-noise about 3:1 or DL = 3.3σ/S |
| Quantitation limit (QL/LOQ) | Lowest amount that can be quantified with suitable precision and accuracy | Signal-to-noise about 10:1 or QL = 10σ/S |
| Robustness | Reliability when method conditions vary slightly (pH of mobile phase, temperature, flow rate) | Studied during development (Q14) |

(σ = standard deviation of the response; S = slope of the calibration curve.)

**Which characteristics for which test**

| Type of test | Specificity | Accuracy | Precision | Linearity/range | DL | QL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Identification | Yes | No | No | No | No | No |
| Impurities – quantitative | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Yes |
| Impurities – limit test | Yes | No | No | No | Yes | No |
| Assay (content, dissolution) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | No |

**System suitability tests** (for example resolution, tailing factor, plate count and repeatability of replicate injections in HPLC) are run with each analysis to show the system works on the day.

## 5.8 Warehousing: good warehousing practice (GWP)

A warehouse stores raw materials, packing materials and finished goods under conditions that keep their quality, and makes sure the right material goes out.

**Principles of GWP**

1. **Adequate space and design:** separate areas for receipt, quarantine, sampling, approved stock, rejected, returned and recalled goods; loading bays protected from weather.
2. **Storage conditions:** as stated on the label (room temperature, "store below 25 °C", 2–8 °C cold room, freezer). Warehouses are **temperature-mapped** to find hot and cold spots, and conditions are monitored and recorded continuously with alarms.
3. **Status control:** quarantine, approved and rejected status shown by labels or by a validated computer system.
4. **Stock rotation:** **FEFO** (first expiry, first out), or FIFO (first in, first out) where expiry is the same.
5. **Cleanliness and pest control:** pallets off the floor, gaps from walls, pest control records.
6. **Security:** restricted access; special secure storage for narcotics, psychotropics, high-value and printed materials; flammables in a separate store.
7. **Records:** receipts, issues, stock balance and reconciliation; physical stock checks at intervals.
8. **Handling:** materials not damaged during movement; spills cleaned at once with records; damaged containers segregated.
9. **Dispatch:** check the right product, batch and quantity; suitable vehicles; cold-chain packaging validated.

```text
Warehouse zones

[Receiving bay] -> [Quarantine] -> [Sampling booth] -> [Approved storage]
                                                         |   (FEFO issue)
                                                         v
 [Rejected - locked]   [Returned/recalled - locked]   [Dispensing / Issue]

[Cold room 2-8 °C]   [Flammables store]   [Secure store for controlled drugs]
[Finished goods quarantine] -> QA release -> [Finished goods store] -> [Dispatch bay]
```

## 5.9 Materials management

**Materials management** plans, buys, stores and controls materials so that the right material in the right quantity and quality is available at the right time and lowest total cost.

**Functions:** material planning, purchasing, receipt and inspection, storage, inventory control, issue, and disposal of surplus or obsolete stock.

**Inventory control techniques**

| Technique | Basis | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ABC analysis | Annual consumption value. A items: few items (roughly 10–20%) taking most of the value (roughly 70%); B items: middle; C items: many items of low value | Tight control and frequent review for A items |
| VED analysis | Criticality: Vital, Essential, Desirable | Never run out of vital items (life-saving drugs, critical raw materials) |
| FSN analysis | Movement: Fast, Slow, Non-moving | Find dead stock to clear |
| HML analysis | Unit price: High, Medium, Low | Purchasing decisions |
| SDE analysis | Availability: Scarce, Difficult, Easy | Plan long lead-time items early |

**Key quantities**

- **Economic order quantity (EOQ):** the order size that keeps the total of ordering and holding costs lowest. EOQ = √(2DS/H), where D = annual demand (units), S = cost of placing one order, H = holding cost per unit per year.
  - Example: D = 10,000 units, S = ₹200 per order, H = ₹4 per unit per year → EOQ = √(2 × 10,000 × 200 / 4) = √1,000,000 = 1,000 units per order (10 orders a year).
- **Safety stock (buffer stock):** extra stock kept to cover delays or unexpected demand.
- **Reorder level:** stock level at which a new order is placed = (average daily use × lead time in days) + safety stock.
  - Example: use 100 units/day, lead time 15 days, safety stock 500 → reorder level = 1,500 + 500 = 2,000 units.
- **Maximum and minimum stock levels** set limits so that money is not tied up in excess stock and production never stops.

## Remember

- Calibrate instruments, qualify equipment (DQ → IQ → OQ → PQ), validate processes and methods.
- Calibration uses traceable standards; an out-of-calibration instrument triggers an impact assessment.
- Types of validation: prospective (preferred), concurrent (exceptional), retrospective (historical data), revalidation (after change); lifecycle: design → qualification → continued verification.
- VMP: policy, scope, responsibilities, list of items, acceptance criteria, schedule, change control.
- pH meter: buffers about 4.01, 6.86, 9.18 at 25 °C; slope about 59.16 mV/pH at 25 °C.
- UV-visible checks: wavelength (holmium), absorbance (potassium dichromate), stray light (KCl), resolution (toluene in hexane).
- Method validation (ICH Q2(R2)): specificity, accuracy, precision, linearity, range, DL (3.3σ/S), QL (10σ/S), robustness.
- GWP: zones, status labels, temperature mapping, FEFO, security, records. EOQ = √(2DS/H); reorder level = use × lead time + safety stock.
